issues.legal_issue: A transferee who acquires disputed property while a suit concerning it is pending may be joined and heard to protect the acquired interest, and may raise a court-fee objection where the applicable law gives defendants that right.
material_facts: The respondent purchased the disputed property after the plaintiffs had presented their suit concerning that property.
The respondent was impleaded as a defendant and challenged orders relating to the plaint’s delayed representations and deficient court fee.
The applicable state court-fee law expressly allowed a defendant to plead that the fee paid was insufficient and allowed an appellate court to consider the correctness of an order affecting the fee.
issues.conclusion: The respondent was entitled to participate to protect his interest and to raise the court-fee issue under the applicable state law, although a defendant cannot succeed in the suit solely because the plaintiff paid insufficient court fee.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, a transfer during a suit concerning immovable property remains valid but is subject to the rights determined in the suit. A pendente lite transferee may be impleaded and heard to protect the acquired interest: Jayaram Mudaliar v. Ayyaswami, Smt. Saila Bala Dassi v. Smt. Nirmala Sundari Dassi, the decision reported at (2005) 11 SCC 403, and Sanjay Verma v. Manik Roy. Sections 12(2) and 12(4)(a) of the Tamil Nadu Court Fees and Suits Valuation Act, 1955 permit a defendant to raise an insufficiency objection and permit appellate scrutiny of the relevant order; the objection does not give the defendant a right to succeed on the merits merely because a fee was deficient.

predicates.property_suit_pending_when_transfer_made: A suit concerning rights in property was pending when the property was transferred.
predicates.transferee_joined_as_defendant: The transferee was made a defendant in the suit to protect an interest acquired from a party to it.
predicates.defendant_entitled_to_raise_fee_issue: The applicable procedural law allowed a defendant to raise the court-fee issue.

issues.definition: When a property suit is pending at the time of transfer, the transferee is joined as a defendant, and defendants may raise the fee issue, the transferee may be heard to protect the acquired interest.

issues.legal_issue: A court may permit a deficient court fee to be paid after the limitation period, and payment cures the deficiency from the date the plaint was first presented if the plaint was originally presented within limitation.
material_facts: The plaint was first presented within the applicable limitation period but with a deficient court fee.
The plaintiffs later paid the deficit court fee after the limitation period had expired.
issues.conclusion: A plaint originally presented within limitation is not necessarily invalid because the court fee was deficient; if the court permits the deficit to be paid, the plaint is treated as having the same force and effect as if the fee had been paid at the outset.
issues.legal_principle: Section 149 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits the court, in its discretion and at any stage, to allow payment of a deficient fee and gives the document the same force and effect as if the fee had been paid initially. It mitigates the operation of Order VII Rule 11 of the Code and Section 4 of the Tamil Nadu Court Fees and Suits Valuation Act, 1955. In Mannan Lal v. Mst. Chhotka Bibi, this Court held that making good the deficiency cures the defect from the date of initial presentation; Mannan Lal approved the relevant Madras Full Bench approach in Gavaranga Sahu v. Batakrishna Patro and considered Faizullah v. Mauladad.

predicates.civil_suit_plaint_presented_within_limit: A plaint in a civil suit was first presented within the limitation period applicable to the suit.
predicates.deficit_court_fee_later_paid: The plaintiff later paid the court fee that was deficient when the plaint was first presented.

issues.definition: If a civil-suit plaint was presented within limitation and the deficient fee is later paid, the plaint is treated as valid from its initial presentation.

issues.legal_issue: Permission to pay a deficient court fee after limitation is discretionary and must not be granted without a legally acceptable explanation for the delay.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought permission to make good the deficient fee after the limitation period had expired.
The explanation for one delay referred to unavailable stamp paper, and no reason was given for another fee deficit.

The explanations for delay included a general claim of jaundice and Siddha treatment, were given in affidavits filed by counsel rather than the plaintiffs, and were accepted without adequate scrutiny.
The High Court set aside the orders condoning the delays, and the Supreme Court found no reason to take a different view.
issues.conclusion: The trial court had not exercised its discretion in accordance with law because it had not been satisfied by a legally acceptable explanation for the delayed payment; the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 149 of the Code of Civil Procedure confers discretion, not an absolute right, to pay court fee later. The court must scrutinize the explanation carefully where the plaint was filed within limitation but the deficit is paid after limitation, because permission can affect defendants’ rights and obligations. The discretion must be exercised according to settled legal principles and is conditional on the court being satisfied that the plaintiff has offered a legally acceptable explanation. The Court relied on P.K. Palanisamy v. N. Arumugham for the discretionary nature of the power.

predicates.civil_suit_plaint_presented_within_limit: A plaint in a civil suit was first presented within the limitation period applicable to the suit.
predicates.deficit_fee_payment_requested_after_limi: The plaintiff asked to pay the deficient court fee after the limitation period had expired.
predicates.legally_acceptable_explanation: The plaintiff gave a legally acceptable explanation for failing to pay the required fee earlier.

issues.definition: For a civil-suit plaint presented within limitation, a request to pay the deficit after limitation is not warranted when the plaintiff has no legally acceptable explanation for the delay.
